Description: Ensure the area around the inverter is cordoned off. Verify no unauthorized personnel have access.
Perform complete LOTO on both AC (Medium Voltage transformer/switchgear) and DC (array combiners/recombiners) sides. Verify zero voltage.
Wait the manufacturer-specified time for DC link capacitors to discharge. Verify zero voltage across DC link before touching anything.
Take extensive high-resolution photos of the entire inverter, AC compartment, breaker, soot patterns, and surrounding environment BEFORE touching anything.
Download all available fault logs, event logs, and high-resolution telemetry data from the local data logger and SCADA system prior to the event.
Download event records and oscillography from the AC protection relay (if external at the MV station) or inverter internal grid monitor.
Collect recent PM (Preventive Maintenance) reports, especially IR (Infrared) thermography reports, torque checks, and previous breaker operations.
Inspect the main AC breaker for the epicenter of the fire. Look for melted terminals, vaporized copper/aluminum, and direction of soot/arc flash propagation.
Check for signs of loose connections (fretting, discoloration prior to the arc). Note if the failure originated at the lug/cable termination or inside the breaker mechanism.
Check for signs of water ingress, vermin, insect nests, dust accumulation, or blocked ventilation filters that could cause overheating.
Test AC cables between the inverter and the MV transformer for insulation breakdown. (Ensure disconnected from sensitive electronics).
Check the torque of surviving connections in the AC compartment to identify systemic under-torquing or thermal cycling relaxation.
Perform insulation resistance testing on the DC side to ensure a severe DC ground fault didn't contribute to the AC side failure.
Carefully remove the failed breaker. Preserve it for potential metallurgical/forensic analysis by the manufacturer (Ingeteam) or a third party.
Open a severe incident ticket with Ingeteam Support. Provide them with the initial photos, serial number, and fault logs.
Determine if the fire started at the terminal (often due to thermal cycling, improper torque). Check history of high temps in recent IR scans.
Determine if internal contacts failed to open under load or short circuit, or if the arc chute failed.
Investigate if there was a significant grid event (voltage spike, short circuit on the MV side) that the breaker attempted to clear and failed.
Thoroughly clean all soot and debris from the compartment using specialized non-conductive cleaners to prevent tracking faults.
Replace the breaker, damaged busbars, cables, and any heat-damaged control wiring nearby.
Perform full pre-commissioning checks (Megger, Ductor) on the new installation before re-energizing.
